A strain of M. oryzae was constructed in which the native PKC1 gene was replaced with an analogue-sensitive PKC1 allele (pkc1AS). This allele could be inhbited by the analogue 1NA-PP1. Global transcriptional profiling of mycelium following selective PKC inhibition identified significant changes in gene expression associated with cell wall re-modelling, autophagy, signal transduction and secondary metabolism.
Mycelium was grown in the presence and absence (control) of the inhibitor 1NA-PP1 for a number of different times up to 24 hours.
A, B and D correspond to three biological replicates.
Number corresponds time in hours of harvesting of mycelium after start of experiment.

Mycelium grown in shaking culture. PKC inhibitor added and samples of mycelium harvested at time intervals of up to 24 hours from which RNA was extracted (for RNA-Seq). Compared with control in which inhibitor was not added to mycelium. Two replicates for each timepoint. RNA-Seq analysis performed using DESeq.
Overall Euclidean distance between samples – POS = inhibitor added, NEG = control.

At 1 hour, there does not seem to be a great amount of difference between the inhibitor treated and control samples (supported by data in table below), but from three hours onwards the inhibitor treated samples cluster together separately from the control samples.
Number of genes differentially regulated at each timepoint (P-value < 0.01)
Venn diagrams showing overlap of differentially genes at timepoints 3-24 hrs.

1122 genes were significantly up-regulated in at least one timepoint and 997 genes were significantly down-regulated in at least one timepoint. Fisher’s exact test was used to look for GO terms that were more commonly represented in these datasets as compared to the genome as a whole. None were found in the up-regulated dataset, but some were found in the down-regulated dataset (see graph below).
Heatmaps were produced using log2 expression ratio between inhibitor treated and control samples for selected groups of genes. Green = up-regulated (higher expression in inhibitor treated samples).
Whole pathway shows up-regulation, except ACC1 (acetyl-CoA carboxylase) which isn’t specific to this pathway.
Most genes are up-regulated by inhibitor addition.
Most genes show small down regulation or little change in expression.
NDE2 – up-regulation T3, T6, T12, T24
Key: Ca_trans = calcium transporter, Ca_binding = calcium / calmodulin binding protein, CaPK = calmodulin / calcium dependent protein kinase, PLC = phospholipase C
MGG_04890 - vacuolar Ca2+ ATPase - up-regulated T12, T24
MGG_07066 - calcium-binding mitochondrial carrier protein – down-regulated T6
SLM1 (Phosphoinositide PI4,5P(2) binding protein) – down-regulated T24
STM1 (Protein required for optimal translation under nutrient stress) - down-regulated T3, T6
Six chitin synthases (CHS) show up-regulation (though mainly not significant). Significant up-regulation from three endochitinases and two chitin deacetylases.

Key: BGS - 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase catalytic subunit, RHO1 - 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase regulatory subunit, CT - chitin transglycosylase, EXG - exo-1,3-beta-glucanase, EBG - endo-beta-1,3-glucanase, E134BG - endo-1,3(4)-beta-glucanase, GAS - Beta-1,3-glucanosyltransferase, AGS - alpha-1,3-glucan synthase, EAG - endo-1,3-alpha-glucosidase
268 genes that are up-regulated at times T3-T24 (see spreadsheet for details)
Genes were annotated and placed into functional categories

35 genes involved in transcription including 22 transcription factors. Of these five were identified as being up-regulated during conidiation and two up-regulated during conidiation, appressorium development and germination by Park et al 2013. One was identified as being highly expressed in planta by Kim et al 2000. 18 genes involved in secondary metabolic pathways, including melanin biosynthesis (as mentioned above). Further evidence of cell stress / death in addition to autophagy genes, there are 19 proteolytic genes including 7 genes from ubiquitin modification pathway and 8 potential F-box proteins that may also be involved in this pathway. Also six stress response / protein folding genes and five involved in DNA repair. There are also 15 genes involved in signal transduction (including pkc1 itself), including 2 other protein kinases (one of these is MPS1), a pH response regulator (homologue of palA Aspergillus nidulans), 3 G-protein coupled receptors (two with CFEM domains), one protein phosphatase and two phospholipases. Also, 10 transporters including six MFS transporters.

RNA samples were obtained for leaf sheaths infected with pmk1AS mutants. 1NA-PP1 was added to inhibit PMK1 activity at 26 h and extracted RNA at 32 h. There are two treatments: minus (control) and plus (Pmk1 activity was inhibited by 1NA-PP1). Three replicates were done for each sample.

Genes that showed significant difference in expression (q-value <= 0.05)
742 genes showed significantly higher expression in minus (control strain), 212 of these had a signal peptide.
715 genes showed significantly higher expression in plus (with inhibitor), 139 of these had a signal peptide.
Of the 12 MEP genes, 10 showed significantly higher expression in minus (control strain).

Of thirty two genes that showed co-regulation with BAS genes / AVR-Pita in leaf spray infection, 23 showed significantly higher expression in minus (control strain), 1 showed significantly higher expression in plus (with inhibitor).

Of 91 genes that showed co-regulation with BAS genes / AVR-Pita in leaf drop infection, 59 showed significantly higher expression in minus (control strain), 2 showed significantly higher expression in plus (with inhibitor).
Known effectors that show higher expression in control strain are BAS2 (MGG_09693), BAS3 (MGG_11610) and BAS4 (MGG_10914), AVR-Pita (MGG_15370), AVR-Pik (MGG_15972) and SLP1 (MGG_10097).

DNA from 8 insertion mutants was pooled and sequenced using Illumina.
We are looking for reads that contain the border sequence and any genomic sequence so insertion sites can be elucidated.
After processing - 161571452 reads (15.76 Gb, average length 97.55 bases)
To identify reads that contain the border sequence of the T-DNA transposon:
1: Split the total reads up into sections that are less than 3.6 Gb (limit for Bowtie index).
2: Index each section as a Bowtie database.
3. Use 20 bases from LB to align against reads from each section using Bowtie (allow one mismatch).
Searching with RB produced no hits, hits were produced from LB, but these reads only contained plasmid sequence.
Use bwa to align reads against plasmid sequence.
[darren@angel transposon_insertion]$ bwa aln pCAMBgfp_sequence.fasta MS1_qtrim_atrim.fastq > MS1_plasmid_alignment.sai
[darren@angel transposon_insertion]$ bwa samse pCAMBgfp_sequence.fasta MS1_plasmid_alignment.sai MS1_qtrim_atrim.fastq > MS1_plasmid_alignment.sam
-F 4 means only include mapped reads in bam file (greatly reduces size in this case)
Following two commands converts bam back to sam and retrieves list of reads that map.

By looking at alignment, I estimated new border positions for inserted T-DNA, (in green on plasmid sequence). I used these new sequences (20 bases, starting 5 bases from estimated border) to search reads (allowing 2 mismatches).
144 reads were found that contained the LB and 408 reads that contained the RB.
Of these 114 LB sequences and 317 RB sequences contained at least 15 bases of M. oryzae genomic sequence.
These were assembled using velvet (kmer size 11).
This produced an extra 17 reads spanning the left border and 62 spanning the right border.
